Overview of the mvgam package

Nicholas J Clark

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/mvgam_overview.Rmd
mvgam_overview.Rmd

mvgam fits Bayesian state-space models to time series, extending the dynamic generalised additive models of Clark and Wells (2023). The observation model is a brms formula (Bürkner 2017). A second formula, trend_formula, adds a latent state that evolves through time. Temporal structure that the covariates do not explain is estimated as part of the latent state. Forecasts carry that structure forward. Stan fits the model. The fitted object works with the post-processing tools of four packages: brms, marginaleffects, loo, bayesplot.

For an observation \(y_{i,t}\) on series \(i\) at time \(t\), with link function \(g\) and a response distribution \(\mathcal{F}\):

\[\begin{align*} y_{i,t} & \sim \mathcal{F}(\mu_{i,t}, \theta) \\ g(\mu_{i,t}) & = \alpha_i + \textstyle\sum_j f_j(x_{j,i,t}) + Z_{i,\cdot} \, \eta_{\cdot,t} \\ \eta_{\cdot,t} & \sim \text{trend process}(\eta_{\cdot,t-1}, \dots) \end{align*}\]

The \(f_j\) are any terms a brms formula accepts: linear effects, smooths (Wood 2017), Gaussian processes, monotonic effects and random effects. The latent state \(\eta\) follows one of the trend processes below. The loadings \(Z\) map it onto the series. Each series has its own state when \(Z\) is the identity. A few shared factors drive many series when \(Z\) has fewer columns than there are series.

What mvgam can model

Every brms family works as the observation model. mvgam adds families for ecological and count data:

Family Use case
tweedie() Non-negative data with many exact zeros
beta_nb() Counts with heavier tails than a negative binomial
com_binomial() Bounded counts that are over- or under-dispersed
occ() Occupancy from repeated detection surveys
nmix() Abundance from repeated counts with imperfect detection
diri(), multi(), categ() Compositions and categorical outcomes
mvn(), mvt() Correlated continuous responses

trend_formula names the latent state with one constructor. It can also hold covariates and smooths that act on the state:

Constructor Latent state Typical use
RW() Random walk Series with no fixed mean
LLT(damped = , season = ) Level with a time-varying slope and an optional season Growth that changes rate or levels off, and seasonal shapes that drift
AR(p = ) Autoregression, including sparse lags such as p = c(1, 12) Momentum and seasonal recurrence
VAR(p = ) Vector autoregression Series that drive one another
CAR() Continuous-time AR(1) Irregular times, and series observed at their own times
ZMVN() Correlated residuals with no time recursion Sites, regions or species
PW() Piecewise linear or logistic growth Trends with changepoints

The constructors share a set of options. cor = TRUE correlates the innovations across series. gr with subgr pools correlation matrices across groups. n_lv sets a number of shared latent factors below the number of series. df gives the innovations Student-t tails. ma = TRUE adds a moving-average term to RW(), AR() or VAR(). The help page of each constructor lists the options it takes. hindcast() and forecast() return the parts of a state through component, such as the level, slope and season of LLT().

mvgam() fits data in long format, one row per series and time. jsdgam() fits joint species distribution models to one row per site and species, with phylogenetic and trait-informed loadings.

Portal rodent captures

portal_data holds monthly captures of four desert rodent species from the Portal Project, a long-term field study in Arizona (Ernest et al. 2018). Trapping follows the lunar cycle. Some months went unsampled, which leaves missing counts. Two covariates come with the counts: minimum temperature (mintemp) and a 12-month moving average of vegetation greenness (ndvi_ma12). We held out the last 12 months of each series to score forecasts.

data(portal_data)
train <- subset(portal_data, time <= 68)
test  <- subset(portal_data, time >  68)

Fitting any model below needs a working Stan installation, through either cmdstanr or rstan; the cmdstanr guide covers the setup.

One species

The Desert Pocket Mouse (PP) is dormant through the colder months. Its captures run from long stretches of zeros to peaks above 20. mvgam_data() checks the counts against the family and plots the series, its distribution and its autocorrelation, with the held-out months in black:

pp_train <- droplevels(subset(train, series == "PP"))
pp_test  <- droplevels(subset(test, series == "PP"))
mvgam_data(pp_train, family = poisson(), y = "captures",
           newdata = pp_test)

The first model relates captures to smooth functions of the two covariates, with no latent state:

fit_gam <- mvgam(
  captures ~ s(mintemp, k = 6) + s(ndvi_ma12, k = 6),
  family  = poisson(),
  data    = pp_train,
  newdata = pp_test,
  silent  = 2
)

Captures in one month carry over into the next beyond anything the covariates explain. The randomised quantile residuals of this model remain strongly autocorrelated at lag 1:

plot(fit_gam, type = "residuals", series = "PP")

The second model moves both smooths into trend_formula, where they act on a latent state that follows an AR(1) process. The observation formula keeps the intercept:

fit_ar <- mvgam(
  captures ~ 1,
  trend_formula = ~ s(mintemp, k = 6) + s(ndvi_ma12, k = 6) + AR(),
  family        = poisson(),
  data          = pp_train,
  newdata       = pp_test,
  silent        = 2
)
summary(fit_ar)
#>  Family: poisson 
#>   Links: mu = log 
#> Formula: captures ~ 1 
#>    Data: pp_train (Number of observations: 68) 
#>  Trends: AR(1); formula: ~s(mintemp, k = 6) + s(ndvi_ma12, k = 6) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; 
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#>

#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS

#>

The latent state absorbs the persistence from one month to the next. The residuals of this fit show no autocorrelation left:

plot(fit_ar, type = "residuals", series = "PP")

pp_check() compares the observed counts with counts drawn from the fitted model. The rootogram shows the model reproducing the distribution of captures, zeros included:

pp_check(fit_ar, type = "rootogram")

conditional_effects() plots each covariate’s effect on the expected count. The marginaleffects functions, such as predictions(), comparisons() or slopes(), work on the fit directly:

plot(conditional_effects(fit_ar, type = "expected"), ask = FALSE)

forecast() continues the latent state from its last estimated values into the held-out months. Without a latent state, the first model forecasts from the covariates alone. Its intervals miss most of the high counts:

fc_gam <- forecast(fit_gam)
fc_ar  <- forecast(fit_ar)
plot(fc_gam)

plot(fc_ar)

compare_scores() scores both forecasts with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), where lower is better. summary() sets the scores out by forecast horizon:

scores <- compare_scores(fc_gam, fc_ar, score = "crps")
summary(scores)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    series eval_horizon fc_gam  fc_ar
#>    <fct>         <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 PP                1  8.38   4.82 
#>  2 PP                2 14.4    9.67 
#>  3 PP                3 NA     NA    
#>  4 PP                4  0.482  1.66 
#>  5 PP                5  6.14   4.07 
#>  6 PP                6  4.48   3.23 
#>  7 PP                7  2.08   1.92 
#>  8 PP                8  0.369  0.803
#>  9 PP                9  1.49   1.71 
#> 10 PP               10  4.43   3.42 
#> 11 PP               11  9.80   7.22 
#> 12 PP               12  9.15   6.64
plot(scores, relative = "fc_gam")

The latent state improves the forecasts. The AR model has the lower CRPS in 8 of the 11 scored months. Its CRPS sums to 45.2 against 61.2 for the smooth-only model. Its 90% intervals contain 11 of the 11 held-out counts. Those of the model without a latent state contain 4.

score() also returns the log score, interval scores and, for several series, energy and variogram scores. lfo_cv() repeats the comparison over many forecast origins by refitting on successively longer windows.

Four species

The four species share the covariates but respond to them differently. The observation formula gives each species its own mean through series. In trend_formula, by = lv_axis() gives each species its own smooths of temperature and vegetation. AR(cor = TRUE) gives each species its own latent AR(1) state, with innovations correlated across species:

fit_cor <- mvgam(
  captures ~ series,
  trend_formula = ~ s(mintemp, by = lv_axis(), k = 6) +
    s(ndvi_ma12, by = lv_axis(), k = 6) + AR(cor = TRUE),
  family        = poisson(),
  data          = train,
  newdata       = test,
  silent        = 2
)

conditional_effects() with series = "all" draws each species’ response to temperature in a panel of its own. The responses differ clearly among species. Captures of PP rise with minimum temperature and those of PB rise at the warmest temperatures, while captures of the two kangaroo rats, DM and DO, fall slightly:

plot(
  conditional_effects(fit_cor, effects = "mintemp", series = "all",
                      type = "expected"),
  ask = FALSE
)

The forecasts come from one joint posterior. Each species keeps its own scale and persistence:

fc_cor <- forecast(fit_cor)
plot(fc_cor)

The forecasts track the held-out counts of all four species. Their 90% intervals contain 43 of the 44 held-out counts.

residual_cor() returns the correlations among the species’ innovations, which measure how strongly the species rise and fall together once temperature and vegetation are accounted for:

rc <- residual_cor(fit_cor)
plot(rc)

The two pocket mouse species, PB and PP, share the strongest correlation, 0.55 (95% interval 0.13 to 0.84). n_lv would instead estimate a few shared latent factors for many species. VAR() would estimate how each species’ state affects the others at the next time step.

Reporting

methods_md() writes the fitted model as Markdown equations with its priors. how_to_cite() returns a methods paragraph and the references for the model’s components:

methods_md(fit_ar, heading_level = 4)

Data

\(\mathrm{captures}\): non-negative integer counts

\(N = 68\) observations, \(S = 1\) series, \(T = 68\) time points

Predictors:

  • \(\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}\): continuous covariate
  • \(\mathrm{mintemp}\): continuous covariate

Model

\[ \begin{aligned} t &\in \{1, \ldots, 68\} \\ \mathrm{captures}_{i,t} &\sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_{i,t}) \\ \log \mu_{i,t} &= \alpha + \mu^{(\eta)}_{i,t} + \eta_{i,t} \\ \mu^{(\eta)}_{i,t} &= f^{(\eta)}_{\mathrm{mintemp}}(\mathrm{mintemp}_{i,t}) + f^{(\eta)}_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}}(\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}_{i,t}) \\ f^{(\eta)}_{\mathrm{mintemp}}(\mathrm{mintemp}) &= \sum_{m=1}^{K_{\mathrm{mintemp}}} \beta^{(\mathrm{mintemp}, \eta)}_m B_m(\mathrm{mintemp}) \\ f^{(\eta)}_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}}(\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}) &= \sum_{m=1}^{K_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}}} \beta^{(\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}, \eta)}_m B_m(\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}) \\ \eta_{i,t} &= \phi_{1} \eta_{i,t-1} + \epsilon^{(\eta)}_{i,t} \\ \epsilon^{(\eta)}_{i,t} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_\eta) \end{aligned} \]

where:

  • \(i\) indexes series, \(t\) indexes time
  • \(\mu_{i,t}\): conditional mean of \(\mathrm{captures}_{i,t}\)
  • \(\alpha\): population intercept
  • \(\eta_{i,t}\): latent state at series \(i\) time \(t\)
  • \(\mu^{(\eta)}_{i,t}\): trend predictor from ‘trend_formula’
  • \(f^{(\eta)}_{\mathrm{mintemp}}\): thin plate regression spline in \(\mathrm{mintemp}\), basis size \(K_{\mathrm{mintemp}} = 6\), smoothing SD \(\sigma^{(s, \eta)}_{\mathrm{mintemp}}\)
  • \(f^{(\eta)}_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}}\): thin plate regression spline in \(\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}\), basis size \(K_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}} = 6\), smoothing SD \(\sigma^{(s, \eta)}_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}}\)
  • \(\epsilon^{(\eta)}_{i,t}\): process innovation, SD \(\sigma_\eta\)
  • \(\phi_{l}\): autoregressive coefficient at lag \(l\)

Priors

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha &\sim \text{StudentT}(3, 1.2, 2.5) \\ \sigma^{(s, \eta)}_{\mathrm{mintemp}} &\sim \text{StudentT}(3, 0, 2.5) \\ \sigma^{(s, \eta)}_{\mathrm{ndvi\_ma12}} &\sim \text{StudentT}(3, 0, 2.5) \\ \sigma_\eta &\sim \text{Exponential}(2) \\ \phi_{1} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) \end{aligned} \]

Every other parameter takes an improper flat prior on its support.

Implementation

Fitted with mvgam 2.0.0 (brms 2.23.2; Stan 2.40.0 via cmdstanr). Hamiltonian Monte Carlo: 4 chains, 1000 warmup + 1000 sampling iterations per chain.

mvgam(
  formula       = captures ~ 1,
  trend_formula = ~s(mintemp, k = 6) + s(ndvi_ma12, k = 6) + AR(),
  data          = pp_train,
  family        = poisson(),
  backend       = "cmdstanr",
  chains        = 4,
  iter          = 2000,
  warmup        = 1000
)
how_to_cite(fit_ar)

Where to go next

  • The data formatting vignette prepares data for mvgam(), including missing values and irregular times.
  • The dynamic factor vignette shares latent states across many series.
  • The VAR article estimates how series drive one another, with impulse responses and variance decompositions.
  • The JSDM article fits multispecies data with jsdgam().
  • The N-mixture article covers detection-error families.
  • The forecast evaluation article compares models with score() and lfo_cv() and combines them with ensemble().
